60.bp: Recommender systems choose which items to show you, and they have a systematic problem: popular items get recommended far more often than niche ones. This matters because it creates a feedback loop—more recommendations mean more users see it, which makes it seem even more popular. The real-world goal is to balance serving what everyone wants with surfacing the hidden gems that matter to particular users.
60.wh: Most systems try to fix this by simply asking 'how do we show more variety?' But popularity bias isn't really about variety—it's rooted in deeper reasons. Popular items genuinely resonate with broad audiences, while niche items serve specific needs. A method that just throws in random diverse recommendations misses the actual cause of the bias and ends up mixing quality with forced randomness, harming both fairness and accuracy.
60.ap: FairLRM uses a large language model (an AI trained on vast text) to understand the *why* behind popularity. It breaks popularity bias into two parts: what makes certain items popular on their own (the items themselves) and what users' personal patterns make them drawn to popular things. The system uses carefully written prompts to ask the language model to reason about both global item popularity and individual user taste, then makes recommendations grounded in that deeper understanding.
60.ww: Language models are trained to reason across many domains and can articulate causes and consequences in natural language. By forcing the model to explicitly decompose popularity bias into item-side and user-side factors, the system stops treating bias as a surface problem ('add variety') and instead models the structural reasons the bias exists. This means recommendations can actually target the root causes rather than just the symptoms.
60.po: The paper demonstrates that FairLRM improves both fairness (less bias against niche items) and recommendation accuracy (people get better suggestions) compared to previous methods, because it's addressing the real mechanisms behind the bias rather than working around them.

61.bp: Recommender systems using reinforcement learning watch user behavior in real time—clicks, ratings, how long someone engages—and use that to improve recommendations. This online learning is powerful because systems adapt moment by moment. But it creates a privacy nightmare: collecting behavioral traces reveals detailed patterns about what someone likes, wants, and fears.
61.wh: The tension is fundamental: online learning needs fresh user data to improve, but collecting and storing that data exposes individuals to privacy breaches or misuse. Standard privacy tools like differential privacy (adding noise to mask individuals) tend to degrade the quality of the system significantly. And even if the central system is private, once you've collected the data, it's vulnerable.
61.ap: FeedGuard uses several layers. First, it improves the learning system itself by using a 'critic'—a separate model that validates whether learned behaviors make sense—to guide the main recommendation model. Second, it collects feedback through split federated learning, meaning some computation happens on the user's device before data is sent. Third, it applies differential privacy throughout, which mathematically guarantees that no individual's data leaks, and proves those guarantees formally.
61.ww: By splitting the work between user devices and servers, and adding mathematical privacy noise that can be proven to prevent re-identification, the system removes the central database of user behavioral traces that was the original privacy risk. The critic guidance helps because the learning process needs less data to work well, so less data needs to be collected.
61.po: Experiments show FeedGuard maintains strong recommendation and learning performance in both offline and online settings while meeting formal privacy guarantees—meaning it actually solves the tradeoff rather than just reducing harm.

62.bp: When brands advertise online, they want their ads appearing next to content that reflects their values and image. A luxury brand doesn't want to appear next to violent content; a family-friendly brand doesn't want to appear next to adult material. Automated systems need to scan vast amounts of content and catch these mismatches before ads run, because manual review at scale is impossible.
62.wh: Simple approaches like keyword matching fail because real problems are subtle. A story might have a brief adult scene that's plot-relevant but still problematic for certain brands. Or it might discuss sensitive topics thoughtfully but still disqualify itself. Existing AI models trained on general internet text don't understand these brand-specific safety rules, and there's no good dataset to train on because nobody has systematically collected examples.
62.ap: The paper creates the first large dataset by taking 51 complete stories from Wattpad, breaking them into 435 chapters, and having human raters label each across nine standard safety categories. They then test three approaches: using ChatGPT and GPT-3 with zero training (just asking them to classify), fine-tuning RoBERTa (a specialized model), and fine-tuning GPT-3 with the new labeled data.
62.ww: Models trained specifically on brand-safety examples learn what the subtle patterns actually are, whereas off-the-shelf AI models have never seen examples marked as brand-unsafe. Even though ChatGPT is powerful, it makes mistakes on edge cases because it wasn't designed for this problem. RoBERTa's architecture turns out to be particularly good at picking up the linguistic patterns in safety-critical content.
62.po: The paper shows that fine-tuned RoBERTa outperforms all others, and that the new dataset enables much more reliable automated brand-safety checking. It also reveals which safety categories are harder (general ones like 'violence' are easier than nuanced concerns like 'substance use implications'), helping platforms prioritize where human review is still needed.

63.bp: Modern websites and apps are filled with images and text together—product pages show both pictures and descriptions, social media mixes photos with captions. Recommender systems need to understand all of this together to suggest things people actually want. But pictures contain more than just the item itself: they have backgrounds, decorations, watermarks—noise that distracts from what actually matters.
63.wh: Existing systems treat all parts of an image equally. If you're recommending shoes, the system looks at the shoe, the background, the model wearing it, any logos, all mixed together. This muddles the signal—the background might be more visually distinctive than the shoe itself, so the system ends up learning to match 'shoes in beach settings' rather than 'shoes with similar style.' With text the same thing happens: a product description might mention the brand or marketing phrases more prominently than the actual item properties.
63.ap: TargetMR separates the wheat from the chaff. For text, it uses syntactic parsing (breaking sentences into parts of speech) to identify which words describe the item itself versus flavor text. For images, it uses segmentation (computer vision technique that identifies separate objects in a picture) to isolate the main item from the background. Then it uses a language model to validate which objects are truly central to the item's identity. Once identified, the system refines how it represents these target elements to emphasize the semantic match.
63.ww: By explicitly separating core content from decoration, the system can focus its learning on what actually determines recommendations. A shoe's style matters; the beach background doesn't. A shirt's material and color matter; the brand mention in the text is secondary. The system becomes more faithful to the actual item properties and less distracted by presentation.
63.po: TargetMR can be plugged into any existing recommendation system (Graph Neural Networks or language models) and improves their performance by reducing the semantic shift—the misleading signal—that comes from auxiliary objects. This means recommendations more accurately reflect what users actually prefer about items.

64.bp: People seeking deep answers often need to search through multiple complex documents—research papers with figures and equations, financial reports with charts and tables, technical manuals with diagrams. Current AI systems can answer questions from web text but essentially ignore all the visual information, missing half the knowledge. The real-world need is to let AI genuinely think through documents the way a human analyst would.
64.wh: Visual information in documents (charts, equations, tables, diagrams) isn't optional—it often contains the key insight. But extracting meaning from these requires understanding both what the visual shows and how it relates to the surrounding text. Simple approaches that treat documents as text-only or that try to convert images to text lose the semantic richness. And retrieving the right parts of a 100-page document when you have 50 figures and 200 tables requires understanding granularity—sometimes you need a single figure, sometimes an entire chapter.
64.ap: Doc-Researcher has three layers. First, a sophisticated parser that reads document structure (columns, sections, order of elements) and breaks documents into multiple levels: individual figures, groups of figures, sections, whole documents. Second, a retrieval system that can search across text-only, vision-only, or hybrid combinations, and dynamically chooses how detailed to be based on the query. Third, a multi-agent reasoning loop where different agents decompose a complex question, each gathers relevant evidence from the parsed documents and figures, and then synthesizes a final answer that weaves together insights from multiple sources.
64.ww: By preserving structure during parsing and enabling granular retrieval, the system can find exactly the right evidence. By using multiple agents that each specialize in gathering evidence and then combining their findings, it avoids the trap of a single-path reasoning that might miss something. The visual-semantic understanding from parsing means charts and equations become searchable and interpretable, not just decoration.
64.po: The paper introduces a benchmark with 158 expert-curated questions requiring multi-document, multi-modal reasoning, and shows that Doc-Researcher can answer these correctly more often than baselines that ignore visual information. This enables AI systems to actually think through the kinds of documents humans use for research and analysis.

65.bp: Every video uploaded to social media, every photo in cloud storage, every sensor stream from autonomous vehicles or drones produces massive amounts of data. Storing and transmitting all this is expensive. Lossless compression—squeezing data down without losing any actual information—is the standard solution, but no single compression method works well for all types of data (video, images, sensor streams vary wildly in their structure).
65.wh: The challenge is that different data types have different patterns. A video's entropy (how 'random' or unpredictable it is) might be low because frames are similar, but a sensor stream's entropy might be much higher. Adaptive methods that work well for one type of data often waste computation on types where it's overkill. Also, data distributions shift—the videos on Monday look different from videos on Saturday—so a system trained once becomes stale.
65.ap: MoE-LC uses a 'mixture of experts' approach: train multiple different compression engines (experts), each good at different types or difficulties of data. A routing system estimates how hard a given piece of data is to compress (its entropy) and decides how many experts to activate and which ones. Within the active experts, high-precision calculation happens only in the most important computational steps, while less critical operations use lower precision to save resources.
65.ww: By having specialized experts and routing based on estimated difficulty, the system avoids wasting powerful compression on easy data and avoids using weak compression on hard data. By allowing the routing to change per batch, it adapts to distribution shifts. By focusing high-precision computation only where it matters, the system runs efficiently without sacrificing compression quality on the data types that need it.
65.po: Experiments show MoE-LC achieves 5-70% improvement in compression across real-world multimodal datasets (depending on type), meaning data can be stored and transmitted more efficiently while staying perfectly lossless.

66.bp: Graph theorists and computer scientists care deeply about whether graphs have certain mathematical properties—is there a path visiting every node exactly once (Hamiltonian), can the graph be drawn on a flat surface without crossing edges (planar), does it contain certain forbidden structures (claw-free). These properties are hard to compute directly, but if you visualize a graph as a picture, sometimes humans can see the answer intuitively. The goal is to teach AI systems to detect these properties the way vision works.
66.wh: Graphs can be drawn many different ways. The same logical structure looks wildly different depending on where nodes are placed. Previous vision-based approaches used a single fixed drawing method—say, always arranging nodes in a circle. But some properties are easier to spot in certain layouts than others. A Hamiltonian cycle is obvious in one layout but invisible in another. So the fixed layout becomes a bottleneck, limiting what the vision system can actually learn.
66.ap: VSAL dynamically generates the best visualization for each graph. Rather than using a single standard layout, it has a generator that, for each graph instance, produces a layout optimized to make the property being tested visually obvious. Then a vision model processes that adaptive visualization to detect the property.
66.ww: By allowing the layout to change based on the graph's structure, the system can highlight relevant patterns. If you're checking for a Hamiltonian cycle, the layout can emphasize the cycle structure. If you're checking planarity, it can spread nodes to make crossing issues visible. The vision model no longer fights against a bad visualization; instead, the visualization cooperates with the property being detected.
66.po: VSAL outperforms previous vision-based methods on Hamiltonian cycle, planarity, claw-freeness, and tree detection tasks, demonstrating that adaptive visualization genuinely helps AI systems detect graph properties more accurately.

67.bp: Medical question answering—when a patient asks 'can I take this drug with this condition?'—is high-stakes. Wrong answers can harm people. Language models can write fluent answers to anything, but they hallucinate (confidently state false medical facts). To make medical AI trustworthy, answers must be both accurate and *verifiable*—traceable to real medical knowledge that an expert can check.
67.wh: Language models learn patterns from text but don't truly reason about causality or constraints. A medical knowledge graph—a structured database of diseases, symptoms, drugs, and their relationships—contains the real causal facts, but language models don't naturally respect these constraints when generating text. If a knowledge graph says drug X contradicts condition Y, a language model might still confidently recommend X anyway, or it might stretch logic in ways that sound plausible but are wrong.
67.ap: GC-DPG works in two phases. Phase one: given a user question and a disease-centric knowledge graph, the system plans which facts from the graph are relevant and which intents (seeking symptoms, drugs, tests, diet advice) the question addresses. This creates a structured answer plan that explicitly lists permissible knowledge graph facts. Phase two: the system generates a prompt for the language model that hard-constrains it to only those permissible facts, then runs a bidirectional checker that verifies the generated answer respects the knowledge graph relationships and flags hallucinations.
67.ww: By forcing the language model to plan against the knowledge graph before generating, the system prevents it from freely confabulating. By then constraining generation to the plan and checking consistency bidirectionally, it catches deviations. The knowledge graph provides the ground truth, and the language model is reduced to a translator—it explains graph facts in natural language rather than inventing facts.
67.po: On a Chinese medical QA dataset, GC-DPG improves the precision of mentioned entities and substantially reduces hallucinations compared to models that either ignore the knowledge graph or use it loosely, making it more trustworthy for clinical settings.

68.bp: Online education platforms track student interactions—which problems they attempt, how long they spend, whether they get answers right—to personalize learning. The system needs to infer each student's knowledge state (what they've mastered, what they're struggling with) from their behavior patterns. Better inference means better recommendations for what to study next.
68.wh: Student learning is complex: it unfolds over many timescales simultaneously. Some struggles are short-term confusion that resolves with practice. Some are long-term knowledge gaps. Some patterns show up quickly; others only emerge after weeks. Existing systems use a single architecture (like self-attention) with fixed biases toward certain patterns. Self-attention naturally picks up overall trends and semantic relationships but can miss fine-grained temporal details. Other architectures each have their own characteristic blindspots.
68.ap: FA-KT combines four different model architectures—self-attention, Mamba (a modern efficient architecture), CNN (convolutional networks), and LSTM (recurrent networks)—each of which naturally emphasizes different frequency patterns in data. A frequency-aware router analyzes each individual student's interaction sequence, detects whether it contains more short-term noise or long-term patterns, and dynamically weights the experts accordingly. For a student with high short-term variation, it leans on architectures good at capturing that; for a student with stable long-term trends, it activates different experts.
68.ww: Different architectures truly do capture different frequency components: self-attention emphasizes global low-frequency patterns, CNNs pick up local structures, LSTMs track temporal flow. By explicitly routing based on the frequencies present in each student's data, the system never forces a square peg into a round hole. The personalization per student, rather than using one-size-fits-all, lets each architecture shine where it's actually best.
68.po: Across five benchmark datasets, FA-KT outperforms 20 strong baselines at predicting student performance, indicating that the multi-expert adaptive routing genuinely captures the diversity of learning behaviors better than any single architecture could.

69.bp: Real-world graphs—social networks, financial transaction networks, citation networks—scale to millions of nodes and billions of edges. Training neural networks on these graphs to predict properties or classify nodes is computationally expensive and often impossible on available hardware. The solution is to compress a large graph into a smaller surrogate that preserves the most important structure, so training becomes feasible.
69.wh: Previous graph compression methods work well for undirected graphs (where connections are symmetric: A-B means B-A) but fall apart on directed graphs (where A→B doesn't imply B→A). Directed graphs encode causal structure—transaction flows, cause-effect in citations, influence direction in social networks. Losing directionality in compression means losing the meaning. Also, large directed graphs often have internal community structure (clusters of densely connected nodes); destroying this structure during compression breaks the meaningful patterns.
69.ap: Dir-GD uses community detection to first partition a large directed graph into independent subgraphs (communities). Each subgraph is small enough to train a directed graph neural network on separately. The trained models are then aggregated into a single compact synthetic directed graph that represents what all the local models learned. This synthetic graph is far smaller than the original but tries to capture the essential topology and directional semantics.
69.ww: By respecting community structure, the method avoids destroying the local patterns that matter. By training separately on each community and then synthesizing a global graph, it ensures that directionality is preserved (a→b in a community stays a→b, not symmetrized). The distributed training becomes tractable because individual communities fit in memory, and the synthesis step produces a compact model that still encodes what the original graph's structure teaches.
69.po: On large-scale datasets like soc-pokec-relationships (millions of nodes), Dir-GD achieves over 91% accuracy while compressing to 0.1% of the original size, meaning expensive neural network training becomes feasible on limited hardware while preserving the directed graph structure that applications like fraud detection depend on.

70.bp: Before autonomous vehicles become widespread, they must be tested exhaustively in simulation. But here's the trust problem: when a company submits simulation logs to regulators claiming 'our car is safe, here's the evidence,' how can regulators be sure the logs haven't been faked or altered? And companies don't want to reveal their simulation data because it's proprietary. The goal is cryptographic proof that a simulation ran safely, without exposing the data.
70.wh: Normal verification means auditors inspect the actual simulation logs—but this exposes sensitive data and invites tampering accusations. You could hash the data to prove it existed, but hashing doesn't prove the simulation actually followed safety rules (collision avoidance, speed limits). You need proof that the simulation adhered to specific constraints without revealing the simulation itself.
70.ap: ZK-V uses Zero-Knowledge Proofs (a cryptographic technique where one party mathematically proves a statement is true without revealing the information underlying it) combined with blockchain (a distributed ledger that records and timestamps verifications). A developer simulates their autonomous vehicle and generates a zero-knowledge proof that the simulation satisfied constraints like collision avoidance and speed limits. The proof is recorded on a blockchain, creating a tamper-evident timestamp. A regulator can verify the proof mathematically without ever seeing the actual simulation logs.
70.ww: Zero-knowledge proofs exploit mathematical properties: a prover can construct a proof that a statement is true (e.g., 'this simulation had zero collisions') that's cryptographically sound—faking it is computationally infeasible—without revealing the underlying data. Blockchain creates an immutable record of when the proof was generated, preventing backdating. Together, they create trust: regulators can verify safety happened, companies keep data private, and neither party can fake the proof.
70.po: The paper outlines a simulation-agnostic architecture that works with any autonomous driving simulator and any safety constraint that can be formally expressed, offering a scalable pathway for decentralized, trustless certification in autonomous vehicle deployment.

71.bp: Skin-toned emojis—the skin tone modifier system (yellow, light brown, medium brown, dark brown, very dark brown)—lets people express identity and feel included in digital communication. But AI models that power recommendation, content moderation, and communication features can be biased in how they treat these emojis, effectively discriminating based on skin tone. The goal is to measure and expose these biases so platforms can fix them.
71.wh: It's not obvious that models have tone-based bias in emojis. Specialized emoji models and large language models have seen millions of emoji uses in training data, so they should understand them. But 'understanding' is subtle: a model might associate certain skin tones with certain sentiment (darker tones with negative words), or it might treat the same emoji with different skin tones as completely different entities rather than variations of the same concept.
71.ap: The paper evaluates two types of models: specialized emoji embedding models and four large language models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen, Mistral), analyzing how they represent skin-toned emojis across four dimensions. First, semantic consistency: does the same emoji with different skin tones have related meanings? Second, representational similarity: do different skin tones cluster reasonably or are they treated as unrelated? Third, sentiment polarity: are certain skin tones associated with negative sentiment? Fourth, core biases: across all dimensions, do patterns of bias emerge?
71.ww: By measuring multiple dimensions, the analysis goes beyond surface coverage ('does the model know the emoji exists?') to deeper semantic properties. If a model doesn't treat 😊 (yellow) and 😊🟤 (dark brown) as related, it's missing something fundamental. If darker tones correlate with negative sentiment, that's a representational harm. The comparison across model types exposes which classes of AI systems have worse problems.
71.po: The paper finds that specialized emoji models have severe deficiencies in skin tone modifier support, while large language models handle them better but still exhibit skewed sentiment and inconsistent meanings across skin tones. This identifies specific harms that platforms need to audit and fix to ensure AI treats people equitably.

72.bp: Social media platforms have enormous power to shape public opinion through their recommendation and content filtering policies. A small algorithmic change—amplifying a certain viewpoint or suppressing certain content—can shift which information spreads and cause polarization. Testing these policies requires understanding how users and the platform's algorithms interact, which currently happens through A/B testing (deploy, observe, hope nothing bad happens). The goal is to pre-evaluate policies safely before deployment.
72.wh: A/B testing identifies problems only after they've harmed real people. Creating a test where you intentionally amplify polarization or misinformation just to see what happens is ethically problematic. Simulations of social dynamics are hard: users aren't robots following rules; they respond to others' behavior, change their minds, react to platform interventions. A simulation that doesn't capture this realism will give wrong predictions.
72.ap: PolicySim uses language models to simulate the bidirectional dynamics: user behavior and platform policy influence each other. User agents are tuned via supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to behave realistically on the specific platform. An intervention module uses a contextual bandit (a decision algorithm that balances exploration with exploitation) combined with message passing through the social network to model how platform policies dynamically adapt to network structure. The system runs multiple simulation runs to measure how a proposed policy affects echo chambers, polarization, and information diversity.
72.ww: By using language models trained on platform-specific behavior data, the simulation captures nuance—users don't just click or not click; they respond contextually and sometimes change their minds. By modeling platform interventions dynamically via bandits, the simulation avoids the unrealistic assumption that policies are static. By running multiple runs, it captures variance. This enables pre-deployment prediction of policy impacts.
72.po: PolicySim enables proactive assessment and optimization of intervention policies before deployment, potentially preventing real-world harms from misguided algorithmic decisions and giving platforms a tool to understand the societal impact of their choices.

73.bp: Graph neural networks trained on large datasets learn powerful representations of graph structure and have become standard tools for predicting node properties (like classifying users in a social network). However, machine learning systems can amplify societal biases—a network model trained on historical data might discriminate against people of certain demographics. The goal is to make pre-trained graph models fair with respect to multiple demographic attributes simultaneously (gender and race, or age and income, not just one).
73.wh: Real people have multiple overlapping identities. Existing fairness methods typically protect against discrimination on a single attribute (gender or race), but overlook intersectionality—a person of color and a woman faces a compounded bias that neither attribute alone predicts. Also, making a pre-trained model fair usually means retraining the whole thing, which is expensive and impractical. You need a lightweight solution that works with off-the-shelf models.
73.ap: MultiFPT injects fairness into a pre-trained graph neural network without retraining it. In the first stage, it adds 'prompts'—additional input signals—to the graph that encode fairness constraints and nudge the model toward fair representations. In the second stage, a lightweight adapter network is attached to the pre-trained model and regularized using HSIC (Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion), a statistical test that measures whether node representations are independent of demographic attributes. The adapter is trained to enforce this independence across all sensitive attributes simultaneously.
73.ww: Prompts guide the pre-trained model toward fair representations without modifying its weights. The adapter acts as a fine-grained filter that enforces independence from multiple sensitive attributes at once, rather than optimizing fairness for one attribute at a time. HSIC is a principled measure of independence that works for multiple attributes, avoiding ad-hoc fairness definitions. Together, they achieve fairness without expensive retraining.
73.po: Experiments show MultiFPT reduces bias by approximately 30% on average while maintaining competitive accuracy in node classification tasks, demonstrating that multi-attribute fairness in graph neural networks can be achieved efficiently via prompt tuning and statistical regularization.

74.bp: Personalized AI recommendation systems need to adapt as user preferences change over time. Someone might stop liking sci-fi and start liking romance; dietary restrictions change; career shifts change what kind of content is relevant. The system needs to update recommendations to reflect these preference shifts. But if you're using a large language model as the recommender backbone, updating it is expensive and tricky—you risk forgetting how to handle other users or breaking the parts that were working well.
74.wh: Global fine-tuning (retraining the entire model on new data) changes everything at once, perturbing recommendations for users whose preferences haven't shifted. Pointwise editing (updating one user's preference at a time) captures specific changes but misses the broader pattern—if a user shifts from sci-fi to romance, that's more than one preference change; it's a coherent shift. Also, repeated edits interfere with each other—editing user A's preferences might undo what you did for user B. This is called catastrophic forgetting.
74.ap: RAIE (Region-Aware Incremental Editing) freezes the backbone language model and instead modifies Low-Rank Adaptation modules—lightweight parameter sets that act like detachable editing layers. It first partitions the representation space into semantic regions using spherical k-means (grouping similar user preference patterns together). When a user's preferences change, the system identifies which region they belong to, then performs one of three region-level edits: Update (refine the region for changed preferences), Expand (grow the region to cover related items), or Add (introduce a new region for novel preferences). Each region has its own LoRA module trained only on that region's data.
74.ww: By working at the region level rather than globally or pointwise, edits are focused without being overly narrow. A region gathers users with similar preferences, so updating one region doesn't disturb others. Because each region has its own LoRA module and is trained independently, regions don't interfere with each other, avoiding catastrophic forgetting. Confidence-aware gating ensures users are routed to the right region even as preferences drift.
74.po: RAIE enables incremental preference updates in LLM-based recommenders while maintaining stable, consistent recommendations across sessions, solving the core problems of both global update (over-perturbation) and pointwise update (interference and narrow coverage).
